opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the easiest way to see it is to look at where the interesting engineering work has actually been moving. A few years ago, if you wanted better behavior out of a system, the lever you pulled was the model: more data, better pretraining, a better post-training recipe. Then there was a phase where people got really into prompting, and that was kind of the first hint that there was a layer above the weights that mattered a lot. But a prompt is a pretty thin thing. What we have now is much thicker. The harness is the loop that decides what the model sees, which tools it can call, how results get fed back, when context gets compacted or summarized, how memory persists across sessions, how permissions work, when to spawn sub-agents, when to stop. That's a real piece of software with its own design space, and it has a huge effect on outcomes.

The thing that convinced me it's a distinct layer, and not just "application code," is that the same model in two different harnesses can look like two completely different products. You see benchmark numbers swing by double digits on agentic tasks just from changing the scaffold: how tool outputs are truncated, whether the model gets a scratchpad, how errors are surfaced. If a component can move your results that much independently of the weights, it deserves to be treated as a first-class part of the stack, with its own abstractions, its own evals, its own best practices.

And there's a co-design story too, which I think is the really interesting part. Models are increasingly trained inside harnesses. The RL environments look like the deployment environments, so the model learns the conventions of the loop it'll live in: how to use a file-editing tool, how to manage its own context, how to recover from a failed command. So the harness isn't just wrapping the model after the fact; it's shaping what the model becomes. That's analogous to how compilers and hardware co-evolved, or how operating systems and applications grew up together. You get an interface, and both sides start optimizing against it.

So if I draw the stack, I'd put hardware and kernels at the bottom, then the model and its training, then inference serving, and then this harness layer sitting between the raw model and the actual task or user. Its job is to turn a next-token predictor into something that can act over long horizons, reliably and safely. I think a lot of the next couple of years of progress will come from people taking that layer seriously as an engineering discipline rather than treating it as glue code.

r002.rationale: It says changing the scaffold can substantially change agent benchmark results, showing that harness tuning can improve task performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that for a long time the stack was pretty clean. You had hardware, you had the framework layer, PyTorch or JAX, you had the model, and then you had some thin application code on top that called the model. And the model was basically the product. Whatever intelligence you got out of the system was whatever the weights gave you.

What changed is that we started asking models to do things over many steps. Not "answer this question," but "go fix this bug," "go research this topic," "go operate this browser for twenty minutes." And the moment you do that, a whole set of questions shows up that the model itself doesn't answer. What tools does it have access to? How does it see the results? What happens when the context fills up? How do you keep it from going in circles? When does it stop and ask versus just keep going? Who decides what it's allowed to do?

None of that is in the weights. It's all in the scaffolding around the weights. And that scaffolding turns out to matter enormously. You can take the exact same model and get wildly different results depending on how you structure the loop, how you manage memory, how you present tool outputs, what you do on failure. We've all seen this. The same frontier model scores very differently on the same benchmark depending on who built the harness.

So to me that's the tell that it's a real layer. It has its own design space, its own failure modes, its own expertise. It's not the model and it's not the application. It's the thing that turns a model into an agent. And I think historically every time something like that showed up, where a piece of glue code turned out to carry a lot of the performance, it eventually got named, got abstracted, and got its own tooling. Operating systems were that for hardware. Frameworks were that for training. I think harnesses are that for agents.

The other reason I'd call it a layer is that it's increasingly where the iteration happens. Training a frontier model is a months-long, enormously expensive loop. Changing how your harness handles context compaction is an afternoon. So a lot of the practical capability gains people are seeing right now aren't coming from new weights, they're coming from better harnesses on the same weights. That's a pretty strong signal that it deserves to be treated as its own thing rather than an implementation detail.

r001.rationale: The response says practical capability gains are increasingly coming from better harnesses using the same weights, shifting attention away from weight changes.

r002.rationale: It says the same model gets different results depending on harness design and scores differently on the same benchmark, indicating harness tuning can improve task performance.

r003.rationale: The response mentions context management and compaction but does not state that harness tuning reduces the tokens needed to perform a task.

astra-6.text:
I think what’s changed is that the model is no longer the whole system you’re building. When you put a model inside an agent, you need something around it that manages the loop: what context it sees, which tools it can call, how it gets feedback, and when it should stop. That’s the harness.

And those decisions have a huge effect on whether the agent actually succeeds. You can take the same model, give it different tools or a different way to manage context, and get very different behavior. So there’s a layer of engineering there that’s distinct from training the model and distinct from building the application’s interface.

The reason I think of it as a new layer in the stack is that those responsibilities recur across applications. Everybody needs some way to manage state, handle failures, and evaluate whether the agent did the right thing. The harness is where those pieces come together—where a model’s capabilities become a system that can reliably do work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key shift is that the model is no longer the whole system. With an agent, the model is one component inside a loop: it takes an action, gets feedback from the environment, and decides what to do next. The harness manages that loop—the tools, the context, the state, and when to stop or ask a human for help.

That becomes a distinct layer because those choices have a huge effect on whether the agent actually succeeds. You can hold the model constant and get very different behavior depending on what information you give it and how you structure its interaction with the environment.

So you now have this engineering surface between the model and the application. The model provides capabilities, and the harness turns those capabilities into something that can reliably carry out a task. That’s why I see it as a layer of the stack in its own right.
